Reproducing Scherrer, Lynch et al. (2023) from dandiset 000691¶

Paper. Scherrer JR, Lynch GF, Zhang JJ, Fee MS (2023). An optical design enabling lightweight and large field-of-view head-mounted microscopes. Nature Methods 20, 546-549. doi:10.1038/s41592-023-01806-1.

Claims. The claims file claims/000691/10.1038-s41592-023-01806-1.yaml was written on 2026-10-20 from the full text of the version of record (main text, figure legends, Methods, Extended Data legends and reporting summary) and the paper's code, GitHub FeeLab/Feescope-Paper-Code at commit d596646, by a reader who did not see the data, and checked by a second reader. It decides what is tested and how. This is the second attempt on the dandiset (000691-scherrer-2023-02); the first (-01) worked from claims written from the abstract and the public legends, and is deprecated.

Dandiset. DANDI:000691, version 0.260827.1358. Why this version: the paper cites no DANDI version (its data statement points to an Academic Torrents deposit), and 0.260827.1358 is the only published version, the one the first attempt used. The draft was last modified when that version was published and holds the same two assets with the same blobs (printed in the data check), so the data have not changed since the first attempt.

What the dandiset holds. One session of one mouse (4 mm cranial window, jGCaMP7f) imaged with the Kiloscope while it explores a square loop maze: the imaging video (consistent with the raw video, see the motion notebook), 2948 EXTRACT footprints with traces and masks, and a behaviour video (a second asset, an AVI). It holds no position of the mouse, no curation of the footprints, no pixel size, and none of the data of the other three mice, the three birds, or the optical tests.

Outside inputs. The claims file places the optical measurements of five claims (bead images, their region lists, and images of a thin layer of dye) in the paper's code repository at commit d596646 (data: elsewhere); they are read from there. Every other result is computed from the dandiset. Method details come from the claims file, which cites the Methods and the code; see the helper module kiloscope.py.

Notebooks of this entry. This notebook holds the data check and every claim but four. The decoding claims are in decoding_quadrant_direction.ipynb (fig2-quadrant-direction-decoding, fig2k-decoder-size, fig2l-local-decoding-map) and decoding_octant.ipynb (ed9b-octant-decoding, ed9c-local-decoding-map), and the motion claim in motion_scherrer_2023.ipynb (ed7-motion-small), each to keep within the time limit. Outputs added after the first verification are in decoding_null_n2_quadrant_direction.ipynb and decoding_null_n2_octant.ipynb (more null decoders of reading n2) and decoding_reduced.ipynb (reduced runs of fig2k, fig2l and ed9c, which decide no outcome).

Random numbers are drawn from a generator per section, each with its own fixed seed.

import time
import warnings
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests
from dandi.dandiapi import DandiAPIClient
from scipy import ndimage
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment

import kiloscope as ks

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 30)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

started = time.time()
urls = ks.asset_urls()
f = ks.open_nwb(urls)
S = ks.load_session(f)
M = ks.read_masks(urls[ks.NWB_PATH], f)
POS = ks.mask_positions(M)
print(f"NWB traces, timestamps and masks loaded in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
t0 = time.time()
# Frames kept for display: four in the opening part the code leaves out, four after it.
SAMPLE_FRAMES = (0, 640, 1280, 1900, 4000, 8000, 12000, 15000)
track, B = ks.load_behaviour(urls, S, keep_frames=SAMPLE_FRAMES)
B_code = ks.behaviour(S["t_img"], S["t_video"], track, unwrap="code")
print(f"behaviour video decoded and tracked in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

Each check of the metadata against the values is stated under its output. The last part of the check gives, for each finding of the first attempt (000691-scherrer-2023-01), whether it is fixed.

Dandiset description says the data come from: the calcium imaging data from our microscope optimized for weight

session_description: This session includes calcium imaging recorded from a head-mounted microscope in a freely moving mouse while simultaneously recording more than a thousand neurons in cortex.
experiment_description: Here we present a fluorescence microscope light path that enables imaging, during free behavior, of thousands of neurons in mice and hundreds of neurons in juvenile songbirds. The light path eliminates traditional illumination optics, allowing for head-mounted microscopes that have both a lower weight and a larger field of view (FOV) than previously possible. Using this light path, we designed two microscopes: one optimized for FOV (~4 mm FOV; 1.4 g), and the other optimized for weight (1.0 mm FOV; 1.0 g). This dataset includes the calcium imaging data from our microscope optimized for weight.For this experiment, we stereotactically located a region of the mouse brain at coordinates associatied with primary visual and somatosensory regions, performed approximately 20 viral injections of GCaMP7f across a 4-mm-diameter region of cortex, and then implanted a 4-mm-diameter glass window in the skull. After letting each mouse recover, we installed our head-mounted microscope and allowed it to freely explore a circular maze while recording calcium activity for several minutes.

The dandiset has one published version, 0.260827.1358, and the draft holds the same assets with the same blobs, so nothing has changed since the first attempt. The device description names the large-FOV microscope (Kiloscope) but gives the size and weight of the other one ("optimized for weight (1.0 mm FOV; 1.0 g)"), and the dandiset description also says the data come from "our microscope optimized for weight". The data are from the Kiloscope: a 4 mm window (the surgery field), thousands of footprints, and frames of 808 x 608 pixels, the size the paper's code uses for the Kiloscope (sf3/widefield/analysis.m). The imaging is stored as a TwoPhotonSeries and the dandiset lists two-photon microscopy, but the microscope is a one-photon head-mounted epifluorescence microscope. The imaging plane gives the indicator and location as "unknown", an excitation wavelength of NaN and no grid spacing (pixel size), although general/virus says GCaMP7f. The plane segmentation has only image_mask and ROICentroids: no column marks the footprints kept by the paper's curation. The only processing module is ophys: there is no position of the mouse, and no interval marks the opening of the behaviour video. The segmentation parameters record cellfind_min_snr = 2, as the Methods state.

def rate_summary(t):
    dt = np.diff(t)
    return {"n": len(t), "first_s": round(t[0], 3), "last_s": round(t[-1], 3),
            "median_dt_ms": round(1000 * np.median(dt), 2), "rate_hz": round(1 / np.median(dt), 2),
            "min_dt_ms": round(1000 * dt.min(), 2), "max_dt_ms": round(1000 * dt.max(), 2),
            "within_10pct": round(float(np.mean(np.abs(dt / np.median(dt) - 1) < 0.1)), 3)}

The imaging runs at a median 29.7 frames/s over 1234 s, as the series description says (about 30 frames/s), with irregular intervals. The behaviour video's timestamps run at a median of 12.5 frames/s over the same 1234 s, while its description says about 30 frames/s and the AVI header says 30 frames/s. The AVI has as many frames as the NWB file has timestamps for it, so the timestamps are taken as the true frame times: at 30 frames/s the AVI would last only 517 s. The traces are stored as "df/F" with unit "n.a."; three quarters of their values are exactly zero, as EXTRACT's non-negative output gives. Every mask has a largest weight of exactly 1, so the code's position (the first pixel of weight 1) exists for every footprint; it equals the stored ROICentroids for 84% of footprints and is within one pixel for the rest; the stored values are described as "the x, y, (z) centroids of each ROI" but equal the rounded weighted centroid for only 43% of footprints (printed above), and how they were computed is not said. The masks are stored transposed relative to the code's arrays (axis 1 is the code's column, of 808).

# Which movie axis each centroid column indexes, and whether traces, masks and movie share a clock.
movie = f[ks.MOVIE]
rng_check = np.random.default_rng(691_00)
active = np.argsort(T[:2400].std(0))[::-1]
picked = active[:6]
controls = rng_check.choice(active[200:], size=6, replace=False)
n_check = 2400
lags = np.arange(-15, 16)

def hp(v):
    return v - pd.Series(v).rolling(301, center=True, min_periods=1).median().to_numpy()

def xcorr(a, b):
    out = []
    for L in lags:
        if L >= 0:
            out.append(np.corrcoef(a[L:], b[:len(b) - L])[0, 1])
        else:
            out.append(np.corrcoef(a[:L], b[-L:])[0, 1])
    return np.array(out)

rows = []
for i, j in zip(picked, controls):
    c0, c1 = S["centroids"][i]
    patch = hp(movie[:n_check, c0 - 2:c0 + 3, c1 - 2:c1 + 3].astype(float).mean((1, 2)))
    own, other = hp(T[:n_check, i].astype(float)), hp(T[:n_check, j].astype(float))
    xo, xc = xcorr(patch, own), xcorr(patch, other)
    rows.append({"footprint": i, "r_own_lag0": round(xo[15], 3), "best_lag_frames": int(lags[np.nanargmax(xo)]),
                 "r_own_best": round(np.nanmax(xo), 3), "r_other_footprint_lag0": round(xc[15], 3)})
print("Movie pixels (5 x 5 at each footprint's ROICentroid, first 2400 frames, slow drift removed) against traces:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

The movie pixels at a footprint's stored position follow its own trace at lag 0 and do not follow another footprint's trace (printed above), so the traces come from this movie on its clock and the positions index the movie as (axis 1, axis 2). These are the six footprints with the most variable traces in the first 2400 frames (80 s); the movie is chunked 1200 frames at a time, and the whole movie is read in the motion notebook.

jump = np.flatnonzero(vstep > 40) + ks.FIRST_VIDEO_FRAME
bad[jump] = bad[jump + 1] = True
B_clean = ks.behaviour(S["t_img"], S["t_video"], dict(track, x=np.where(bad, np.nan, x), y=np.where(bad, np.nan, y)))
same_frames = np.array_equal(B_clean["sel"], B["sel"])
print(f"  without those {bad.sum()} video frames: same imaging frames {same_frames}; imaging frames whose quadrant changes "
      f"{np.mean(B_clean['quadrant'] != B['quadrant']):.4f}, octant {np.mean(B_clean['octant'] != B['octant']):.4f}, "
      f"running {np.mean(B_clean['running'] != B['running']):.4f}, direction {np.mean(B_clean['direction'] != B['direction']):.4f}")
print(f"Running frames (speed above median): {B['running'].sum()}; direction +1 in {np.mean(B['direction'][B['running']] > 0):.3f} of them")
laps = np.flatnonzero(np.abs(np.diff(B["s"])) > B["perimeter"] / 2)
resid = np.abs(np.diff(B_code["sunwrap"]))[laps] * 100
print(f"\nThe code's unwrap (MATLAB unwrap of s * 100 with tolerance max(s) * 100 / 2): at the {len(laps)} wraps of linear "
      f"position it leaves steps of {resid.min():.2f} to {resid.max():.2f} cm (median {np.median(resid):.2f}); the loop unwrapped "
      f"leaves {np.abs(step[laps]).min() * 100:.2f} to {np.abs(step[laps]).max() * 100:.2f} cm; median step between frames "
      f"{np.median(np.abs(step)) * 100:.2f} cm")
print(f"  labels that differ with the code's unwrap: running {np.mean(B_code['running'] != B['running']):.4f}, "
      f"direction {np.mean(B_code['direction'] != B['direction']):.4f}, running and direction (8 classes) among frames "
      f"running in both {np.mean((ks.quad_dir_labels(B_code) != ks.quad_dir_labels(B))[B['running'] & B_code['running']]):.4f}")

The dandiset gives no position, so it is tracked here with the code's rule: frames from 1920 on, rotated by 86.79 degrees and cropped as the code does (the crop equals a full rotation to within one grey level, printed above), and the code's colour rule. The track lies along the code's rectangle (distances printed above), so the rectangle's fixed corners fit this video. The mouse runs about 48 loop lengths and visits every quadrant and octant. No step between consecutive video frames exceeds 40 pixels, and leaving out the 69 frames with a blob under 50 pixels changes the quadrant of 0.03% of imaging frames. The sample frames show the crop and the tracked centroid on the mouse. The 64 s the code skips, 1920 frames at the AVI's nominal rate, are 153 s on the timestamps. The code unwraps linear position with MATLAB's unwrap on centimetres, which corrects each lap's jump by a multiple of 2 pi cm; as the loop (147.1 cm) is not such a multiple, the position gains an error of up to pi cm at every lap. At the 98 wraps its steps are 0.01 to 3.08 cm where the position unwrapped by the loop length steps 0.01 to 4.70 cm (printed above). The claims file says position is unwrapped, which is done here by the loop length; with the code's version, about 1% of the running and direction labels differ (printed above).

# Shared clock of behaviour and imaging: decode the quadrant (4 classes) with labels shifted in time.
rng_clock = np.random.default_rng(691_01)
rate = 1 / np.median(np.diff(S["t_img"]))
act = ks.moving_max(T[B["sel"]])
run = B["running"]
rows = []
for lag_s in [-60, -20, -5, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 5, 20, 60]:
    shifted = np.roll(B["quadrant"], int(round(lag_s * rate)))
    dm = ks.decoding_matrix(act[run], shifted[run], 4, ks.LAMBDA_QUAD_DIR, 3, rng_clock, n_jobs=4)
    rows.append({"label_shift_s": lag_s, "median_accuracy_3_fits": round(dm["median"], 3)})
print("Quadrant decoding (chance 0.25), the average matrix of 3 fits per shift:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

# Footprints deposited twice: pairs with near-identical traces and nearby positions.

np.fill_diagonal(C, 0)

Status of the findings of 000691-scherrer-2023-01, from the output above:

  1. One mouse of four, no bird or optical data: still present (one subject, two assets).
  2. The device description gives the weight-optimized microscope's FOV and weight: still present.
  3. One-photon imaging stored as a TwoPhotonSeries and listed as two-photon microscopy: still present.
  4. The behaviour video described as about 30 fps, with timestamps at 12.5 frames/s: still present.
  5. No pixel size; indicator and location "unknown", no excitation wavelength: still present.
  6. The curated footprints not marked: still present.
  7. No position of the mouse; the opening of the video not marked: still present.
  8. The code's local maps use 64 footprints within 50 pixels where the legend says 32 within 270 um: still present for the number of footprints in both map scripts. The radius differs only at the illumination script's 5.94 um per pixel (297 um); at the bead script's 5.35 um per pixel, 50 pixels are 267.5 um, close to 270 um, so that part of the finding depends on the pixel size.
  9. Extended Data Fig. 8's legend refers to "Figure 3" and to a ridgeline plot in "Fig. 2d" (the ridgeline is Fig. 2h): still present in the version of record's full text, which the first attempt had not read.

New findings of this attempt, shown above and in the claim sections: the stored ROICentroids are closer to the peak pixel than to a weighted centroid, and how they were computed is not said; the code's unwrap gains an error of up to pi cm at each lap; the bead scripts order their images by file date, which the repository does not keep (the Featherscope regions confirm the file-number order); and, in the motion notebook, the movie's rigid shifts against a template are about a quarter of those the paper reports, while nothing says whether the movie is raw or motion-corrected (its values are consistent with the raw video).

abstract-thousands-of-neurons¶

The Kiloscope records thousands of neurons at once in a freely behaving mouse; in the mouse with the best expression EXTRACT gave 2,948 footprints.

Criterion: the number of footprints EXTRACT returned for the one session is within 2948 +/- 295, and the footprints were recorded together in a session of free exploration of the maze.

The code repository holds bead images and dye images (used below), Zemax files and an axicon notebook, but no USAF target images and no ADC recordings. ed6a-curated-footprints is blocked as metadata_insufficient (the data are there, the selection is not marked), fig2d-lman-sparse-bursting as methods_underspecified (no measure of sparse bursting is fixed; its data are also missing), and the others as data_missing. The paper's Academic Torrents deposit lists only this mouse's session in its file list (read outside this notebook, not used for any outcome).

abstract-kiloscope-fov¶

The Kiloscope's field of view is 4.8 x 3.6 mm (about 4 mm in the abstract).

Criterion: the frame's width and height in pixels times the object-plane pixel size; a pixel size stored with the data is used when there is one; otherwise the code's 5.94 and 5.35 um per pixel are the two readings, and the claim is reproduced when both sides are within 4.8 +/- 0.48 and 3.6 +/- 0.36 mm under a reading.

In [12]:

for name, um in [("5.94 um/px (sf3/widefield/analysis.m)", ks.UM_PER_PIXEL_ILLUMINATION), ("5.35 um/px (f2+sf4/wf_analysis_secondorder.m)", ks.UM_PER_PIXEL_BEADS)]:
    long_mm, short_mm = h_px * um / 1000, w_px * um / 1000
    rows.append({"reading": name, "longer_mm": round(long_mm, 3), "shorter_mm": round(short_mm, 3),

Result: reproduced. The file stores no pixel size, so the criterion's two readings from the code apply. Frames of 808 x 608 pixels are 4.800 x 3.612 mm at 5.94 um per pixel and 4.323 x 3.253 mm at 5.35 um per pixel; both sides are within tolerance under both readings, the second only just (4.323 against a lower bound of 4.32, 3.253 against 3.24). The pixel size comes from the code, not the dandiset.

fig1e-featherscope-psf and fig1f-kiloscope-psf¶

The Featherscope's resolution (FWHM of the bead PSF) is about 4 um at the centre of the field of view and 7 um at the edges. The Kiloscope's is about 4 um at the centre and about 5 um at the edges.

Criterion: as in f2+sf4/*_analysis_secondorder.m, each bead region at its listed slice is fitted with the code's rotated 2D Gaussian with second-order pixel correction (1.68 and 5.35 um per pixel); FWHM is 2.355 times each axis's width; radius from the code's centre, beads grouped to the nearest of 0, 100, ..., 500 um (Featherscope) or 0, 250, ..., 1500 um (Kiloscope); centre is the 0 um group and edge the last. Readings: (a) median major-axis FWHM, (b) median minor-axis FWHM, (c) mean major-axis, (d) mean minor-axis. Reproduced when centre and edge are both within 10% of 4 and 7 um (Featherscope) or 4 and 5 um (Kiloscope) under a reading.

The images and region lists are read from the code repository at commit d596646.

In [13]:

stacks, rois = {}, {}
for name, s in psf_setups.items():
    files = sorted((n for n in ks.list_code_dir(s["folder"]) if n.startswith("beads") and n.endswith(".png")),
                   key=lambda n: int(n[5:-4]))
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as ex:
        stacks[name] = np.array(list(ex.map(lambda n: ks.read_png(ks.code_file_url(f"{s['folder']}/{n}")), files)))
    tab = pd.read_csv(ks.code_file_url(s["csv"]))
    tab.columns = ["row"] + list(tab.columns[1:])
    rois[name] = tab
    st = stacks[name]
    print(f"{name}: {len(files)} images {files[0]} to {files[-1]}, each {st.shape[1:]} {st.dtype}, values {st.min()} to {st.max()}; "
          f"{len(tab)} bead regions, slices {tab.Slice.min()} to {tab.Slice.max()}")
    # The order of the images: the regions name their image (Featherscope), and the listed slice should be
    # near the slice where the bead is brightest.
    if tab.Label.str.contains("beads").all():
        named = tab.Label.str.extract(r"beads(\d+)")[0].astype(int) + 1
        print(f"  regions whose label (beadsN) is slice N + 1 in file-number order: {(named == tab.Slice).sum()} of {len(tab)}")
    peak = np.array([[img[r.BY:r.BY + r.Height, r.BX:r.BX + r.Width].max() for img in st] for _, r in tab.iterrows()])
    off = peak.argmax(1) + 1 - tab.Slice.to_numpy()
    print(f"  brightest slice minus listed slice, percentiles 10/50/90: {np.percentile(off, [10, 50, 90])}; within 5 slices: {np.mean(abs(off) <= 5):.2f}")

def psf_fits(name, x_scale="code"):
    s, tab, st = psf_setups[name], rois[name], stacks[name]
    rows = []
    for _, r in tab.iterrows():
        roi = st[int(r.Slice) - 1, r.BY:r.BY + r.Height, r.BX:r.BX + r.Width]
        fit = ks.fit_bead(roi, s["dp"], s["start_at_max"], s["ftol"], s["max_nfev"], x_scale)
        hh, hw = (r.Height - 1) / 2, (r.Width - 1) / 2
        rad = s["dp"] * np.hypot(s["centre"][0] - (r.BY + hh + 1), s["centre"][1] - (r.BX + hw + 1))
        rows.append({"r_um": rad, "slice": r.Slice, **fit})
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    g = s["groups"]
    out["group"] = g[np.abs(out.r_um.to_numpy()[:, None] - g[None]).argmin(1)]
    return out

def readings(fits, name):
    s = psf_setups[name]
    by = fits.groupby("group")
    table = pd.DataFrame({"n": by.size(), "median_major": by.fwhm_major.median(), "median_minor": by.fwhm_minor.median(),
                          "mean_major": by.fwhm_major.mean(), "mean_minor": by.fwhm_minor.mean()}).round(3)
    centre_g, edge_g = s["groups"][0], s["groups"][-1]
    rows = []
    for label, col in [("(a) median major", "median_major"), ("(b) median minor", "median_minor"),
                       ("(c) mean major", "mean_major"), ("(d) mean minor", "mean_minor")]:
        cv, ev = table.loc[centre_g, col], table.loc[edge_g, col]
        rows.append({"reading": label, "centre_um": cv, "edge_um": ev,
                     "centre_within": abs(cv - s["expect"][0]) <= 0.1 * s["expect"][0],
                     "edge_within": abs(ev - s["expect"][1]) <= 0.1 * s["expect"][1]})
    return table, pd.DataFrame(rows)

psf = {}
for name in psf_setups:
    t0 = time.time()
    psf[name] = psf_fits(name)
    fits = psf[name]
    table, read = readings(fits, name)
    print(f"\n{name}: {len(fits)} fits in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; stopped by the evaluation limit: {(fits.status == 0).sum()}; "
          f"FWHM major {fits.fwhm_major.min():.2f} to {fits.fwhm_major.max():.2f} um, minor {fits.fwhm_minor.min():.2f} to {fits.fwhm_minor.max():.2f} um")
    print(table.to_string())
    print(read.to_string(index=False))
    print("  a reading with both within tolerance:", bool((read.centre_within & read.edge_within).any()))

# For each bead, the lower-cost of the two fits (the main fit and the Jacobian-scaled one), the one nearer the
# least-squares minimum that lsqcurvefit seeks.
psf_best = {}
for name in psf_setups:
    main_, jac_ = psf[name], psf_jac[name]
    use_j = (jac_.cost < main_.cost).to_numpy()
    best = psf_best[name] = main_.copy()
    best.loc[use_j] = jac_.loc[use_j]
    _, read_b = readings(best, name)
    print(f"\n{name}, the lower-cost fit for each bead (the Jacobian-scaled fit for {use_j.sum()} of {len(best)} beads):")
    print(read_b.to_string(index=False))
    print("  a reading with both within tolerance:", bool((read_b.centre_within & read_b.edge_within).any()))
    print(f"  largest major FWHM: main fits {np.round(np.sort(main_.fwhm_major)[-3:], 2).tolist()}, lower-cost fits "

Result: reproduced (fig1e-featherscope-psf). Under reading (a) the median major-axis FWHM is 3.919 um at the centre (11 beads) and 6.433 um in the 500 um group (19 beads), within 10% of 4 and 7 um; reading (c) gives 3.887 and 6.883 um (6.884 with Jacobian scaling), also within. The minor axis is narrower (2.609 and 5.203 um under b) and fails at both positions. All 155 regions name their image in file-number order. With Jacobian scaling no bead's major FWHM moves by more than 0.5 um, and taking for each bead the lower-cost of the two fits gives the same readings (3.919 and 6.433 um under a).

Result: partially reproduced (fig1f-kiloscope-psf). No reading puts both values within tolerance, with either optimizer or with the lower-cost fit for each bead. Under (a) the edge (1500 um group, 11 beads) is 5.441 um, within 5 +/- 0.5, and the centre (11 beads) is 4.467 um, 0.067 um above the bound of 4.4. The mean major axis (c) is 4.537 um at the centre and 7.373 um at the edge, where one bead is fitted at 27.77 um; the minor axis gives 2.722 and 3.306 um (b). The fits depend on the optimizer, as the PSF is narrower than a pixel (5.35 um): with Jacobian scaling 15 of 118 beads' major FWHM move by more than 0.5 um and (a) gives 3.639 um at the centre (within) and 5.892 um at the edge (0.392 um above the bound). Taking for each bead the lower-cost fit, the one nearer the least-squares minimum, gives 4.467 and 5.892 um under (a), both outside, and 4.685 and 7.944 um under (c); the 27.77 um edge bead keeps its main fit, which has the lower cost (60.092 against 79.942). These fits are not the same in every execution: the seeds are fixed, but the values printed above differ between runs on different machines (the attempt record gives those of the run reviewed in the second verification, where the lower-cost fits put the centre within tolerance and the edge outside). The listed slice is within 5 slices of the bead's brightest slice for 72% of the Kiloscope's regions, and the image order of that stack is not confirmed by its labels. Under every reading and every fit the FWHM is larger at the edge than at the centre, and under (a) one of the two positions is within tolerance with the main fits (the edge) and with the Jacobian-scaled fits (the centre), so the claim holds in part.

ed1cf-field-curvature¶

Both microscopes have field curvature small enough for typical imaging depths.

The paper gives no bound on field curvature and no typical imaging depth, so no method it fixes decides the claim (methods_underspecified). As the criterion asks, the slice of best focus (the Slice column of the region lists, over the 100 um stack of the Methods) is reported against radius for both microscopes.

Result: blocked (methods_underspecified). The paper sets no bound on field curvature, so nothing decides the claim. As the criterion asks, the slice of best focus is shown: for the Featherscope it rises from a median of 6 at the centre to 89 in the 500 um group (of 161 slices; Spearman 0.96 with radius), and for the Kiloscope it falls from 48 at the centre to 29 in the 1500 um group (of 91 slices; Spearman -0.66). The Methods say the stack spans 100 um; if its slices are evenly spaced, these are about 52 um and 21 um of focal shift across the field.

ed2b-featherscope-flat-illumination and ed2c-kiloscope-flat-illumination¶

With the axicon correction optics the signal profile is flat across the field of view, where total vignetting makes the signal fall toward the edges (Extended Data Fig. 2b for the Featherscope, 2c for the Kiloscope).

Criterion: radial profiles as sf3/*/analysis.m computes them; the corrected profile is the axicons image, total vignetting the reference image, optical vignetting the led image. Edge radius readings 0.5 and 0.45 mm (Featherscope), 1.8 and 2.0 mm (Kiloscope). Reproduced when, under both, the corrected profile at the edge radius is higher than the total-vignetting profile and its fall from the centre is smaller.

The code's profiles run from 0 to rLength - 1 um (499 and 1999 um), so the 0.5 mm and 2.0 mm readings are taken at the last bin, 1 um short; a profile extended to include 500 and 2000 um is shown as a check (a standard choice that cannot change the outcome).

    for label, shift in [("intensity-weighted (main)", (0, 0)), ("+100 um in x", (1, 0)), ("-100 um in x", (-1, 0)),
                         ("+100 um in y", (0, 1)), ("-100 um in y", (0, -1)), ("image centre", None)]:
        row = {"centre": label}
        for R in s["radii"]:
            Rb = min(R, s["r_length"] - 1)
            vals = {}
            for k in ("corrected", "total vignetting"):
                img = images[name][k]
                xc, yc = ks.weighted_centre(img)
                step = 100 / s["um"]
                centre = ((img.shape[1] + 1) / 2, (img.shape[0] + 1) / 2) if shift is None else (xc + shift[0] * step, yc + shift[1] * step)
                p = ks.radial_profile(img, s["um"], s["r_length"], s["med"], centre=centre)
                vals[k] = (p[Rb], p[0] - p[Rb])
            row[f"holds_at_{R}um"] = vals["corrected"][0] > vals["total vignetting"][0] and vals["corrected"][1] < vals["total vignetting"][1]
            row[f"corrected_{R}"] = round(vals["corrected"][0], 3)
            row[f"total_{R}"] = round(vals["total vignetting"][0], 3)
        rows.append(row)
    print(f"\n{name}:")
    print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Result: reproduced (ed2b-featherscope-flat-illumination). At both edge readings the corrected profile is higher than the total-vignetting profile and falls less from the centre: at 0.5 mm (the code's last bin, 499 um) 0.511 against 0.193, falling by 0.470 against 0.814; at 0.45 mm 0.628 against 0.257, falling by 0.353 against 0.750. The bin at 500 um of an extended profile differs by at most 0.005. With the centre moved by 100 um in either axis, or at the image centre, the comparison holds at both radii. The three images are the ones sf3/feather/analysis.m loads, in the same roles (its lines 20 to 22, printed above). The corrected profile still falls to about half its peak at 0.5 mm; the criterion judges it against total vignetting, as the legend does.

Result: reproduced (ed2c-kiloscope-flat-illumination). At 1.8 mm the corrected profile is 0.557 against 0.180 for total vignetting (falling by 0.437 against 0.843), and at 2.0 mm (the code's last bin, 1999 um) 0.420 against 0.148 (falling by 0.573 against 0.875). The comparison holds at both radii for all six centres tried. The three images are the ones sf3/widefield/analysis.m loads, in the same roles (its lines 18 to 20).

ed8-coactive-distributed¶

The correlated activity in each NMF component is driven by footprints spread across the field of view.

Criterion: NMF of the traces into eight components (multiplicative updates, 4 replicates, tolerances 1e-7); each footprint to the component in which its weight ranks highest; footprints of a component are active in its event when their maximum within 25 s of the event time exceeds half their maximum over the recording. Event times: (a) each component's largest temporal weight; (b) the code's 820, 770, 990, 700, 400, 420, 1000 and 410 s, each assigned one to one to the component with the largest temporal weights at those times. Reproduced when every component's event has active footprints in all four quarters of the field of view (split at the midlines of the extent of all footprint positions, positions as for fig2l: the first pixel of weight 1) under both readings.

The curated set of 2,382 is not marked in the dandiset, so all 2,948 footprints are used, the variant the claims file names.

In [21]:
t0 = time.time()
nmf = ks.nmf_replicates(T, 8, 4, seed=691_08)
W, H = nmf["W"], nmf["H"]
group = ks.nmf_groups(H)
t_tr = S["t_trace"]
print(f"NMF in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; errors of the 4 replicates {np.round(nmf['errors'], 3)} (iterations {nmf['n_iter']})")
print("footprints per component:", np.bincount(group, minlength=8).tolist())
ev_a = t_tr[W.argmax(0)]
code_times = np.array([820, 770, 990, 700, 400, 420, 1000, 410])
W_at = W[np.searchsorted(t_tr, code_times)]                  # rows: the code's times; columns: components
rows_, cols_ = linear_sum_assignment(-W_at)
ev_b = np.empty(8); ev_b[cols_] = code_times[rows_]
rows_n, cols_n = linear_sum_assignment(-(W_at / W.max(0)))
ev_b_norm = np.empty(8); ev_b_norm[cols_n] = code_times[rows_n]
print("event times (a), largest temporal weight (s):", np.round(ev_a, 1).tolist())
print("event times (b), the code's times assigned to components (s):", ev_b.tolist())
print("  assignment with each component's weights scaled to their maximum gives the same times:", bool(np.array_equal(ev_b, ev_b_norm)))
print("  temporal weight at the assigned time / component maximum:", np.round(W[np.searchsorted(t_tr, ev_b), np.arange(8)] / W.max(0), 2).tolist())

peak_all = T.max(0)
def events(times, positions):
    pos = positions
    rmid = (np.nanmin(pos[:, 0]) + np.nanmax(pos[:, 0])) / 2
    cmid = (np.nanmin(pos[:, 1]) + np.nanmax(pos[:, 1])) / 2
    quarter = 2 * (pos[:, 0] > rmid) + (pos[:, 1] > cmid)
    rows, actives = [], []
    for c in range(8):
        members = np.flatnonzero(group == c)
        win = np.abs(t_tr - times[c]) <= 25
        act_ = members[T[win][:, members].max(0) > 0.5 * peak_all[members]]
        actives.append(act_)
        q = np.bincount(quarter[act_], minlength=4)
        rows.append({"component": c, "event_t_s": round(times[c], 1), "members": len(members), "active": len(act_),
                     "upper_left": q[0], "upper_right": q[1], "lower_left": q[2], "lower_right": q[3], "all_four": bool((q > 0).all())})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), actives, quarter

results = {}
for label, times in [("(a) largest weight", ev_a), ("(b) the code's times", ev_b)]:
    for pos_label, pos in [("code's position", POS["peak"]), ("centroid (variant)", POS["centroid"])]:
        tab, actives, quarter = events(times, pos)
        results[(label, pos_label)] = (tab, actives)
        print(f"\nEvent times {label}, positions: {pos_label}; events with active footprints in all four quarters: {tab.all_four.sum()} of 8")
        if pos_label == "code's position":
            print(tab.to_string(index=False))
            print("  all footprints per quarter:", np.bincount(quarter, minlength=4).tolist())
        else:
            print("  active per quarter, smallest count over events and quarters:", int(tab[["upper_left", "upper_right", "lower_left", "lower_right"]].to_numpy().min()))

Result: blocked (methods_underspecified). Under event reading (a) every component's event has active footprints in all four quarters of the field of view (8 of 8, with 192 to 326 active footprints). Under reading (b), the code's times, 7 of 8 do: component 1's event at 1000 s has 151 active footprints and none in the lower-left quarter, which holds only 85 of all 2948 footprints. The two readings give different outcomes, so by the criterion the claim is methods_underspecified. The code's times fall where this NMF's components have weights of 0.04 to 0.68 of their maximum, as a new NMF run does not reproduce the code's components. With weighted centroids as positions the counts are the same (8 of 8 and 7 of 8), and with the code's frame window (frames 30 times the times) component 1's event again has none in the lower-left quarter (7 of 8). With the quarters split at the image's midlines (row 304.5, column 404.5) in place of the midlines of the footprints' extent, the lower-left quarter holds 86 of 2948 footprints and the counts are again 8 of 8 under (a) and 7 of 8 under (b), component 1 at 1000 s having none there. Under reading (b), five components' assigned times fall where their temporal weights are 0.04 to 0.13 of their maximum (components 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 are at 0.11, 0.04, 0.06, 0.05 and 0.13), so those times are not events of this NMF run.

ed10-localized-activity¶

Some footprints have activity localized to subregions of the maze.

The paper selected footprints by eye; neither the paper nor the code sets a test for "localized", so the claim cannot be judged by a method the paper fixes (methods_underspecified). As the criterion asks, the maps of place_cells.m and each footprint's entropy and map peak are reported.

Where an outcome differs from 000691-scherrer-2023-01, the claim's criterion changed: the claims file was rewritten from the full text. ed2b and ed2c are now judged against total vignetting, not against a level of 0.8 chosen by the earlier author; abstract-kiloscope-fov now admits the code's pixel sizes; ed8 now asks for active footprints in all four quarters under two readings of the event times; ed10 is now methods_underspecified; ed9b and ed9c now use the paper's null, a thousand decoders on shuffled activity, whose reading with 200 fits per decoder cannot run here.

How the analysis differs from the paper's.

  • All 2948 EXTRACT footprints are used where the claims name the 2,382 curated ones (all 2948 is the claims file's variant); the dandiset does not mark the curated set.
  • Position is tracked from the behaviour video with the code's rule; the paper's tracking output is not in the dandiset. Linear position is unwrapped by the loop length, as the claims file says; the code's unwrap differs in about 1% of labels.
  • MATLAB's fits are replaced: linear SVMs by scikit-learn (SGD with 10 passes for all footprints, as MATLAB's default for more than 100 predictors), lsqcurvefit by scipy's trust-region-reflective least squares, nnmf by scikit-learn's multiplicative-update NMF, NoRMCorre by a rigid registration written after it.
  • The decoding claims' null with 200 fits per shuffled decoder, and the decoder-size and map analyses, need 64,000 to 276,000 fits each and were not run; their cost is measured in the decoding notebooks. Eight more (n2) null decoders per claim, and reduced runs of the decoder-size and map analyses, are in the added notebooks; they decide no outcome.

What was found about the dandiset (with the status of each finding of -01 in the data check): it holds one of four mice and no bird or optical data; the device is described as the weight-optimized microscope; one-photon imaging is stored as two-photon; the behaviour video is described as 30 frames/s but runs at 12.5; there is no pixel size, indicator, location, curation or position; and nothing says whether the movie is raw or motion-corrected. Its values are consistent with the raw video (see the motion notebook), and its shifts are about a quarter of those the paper reports.
